Issued at 201 AM CDT Fri Sep 11 2026

     Dense Fog This Morning...
Early this morning, surface high pressure centered over lower 
Michigan extends southwestward into central Illinois. Light and 
variable winds, combined with clearing skies from the west, have
set the stage for strong radiational cooling. Given the influx 
of low-level moisture from recent rainfall, dense fog has 
developed in several areas. As the ridge axis shifts eastward 
over the next several hours, a developing southeasterly pressure
gradient may act to displace or dissipate the fog from east to 
west. In the interim, a Dense Fog Advisory remains in effect for
portions of central Illinois, specifically from the lower 
Illinois River Valley eastward through Springfield. Will monitor
observational trends closely for any needed expansions through 
mid-morning.

     Upper Low This Afternoon and Evening...
Water vapor imagery early this morning reveals a potent mid- 
level vort max digging southeastward across Oklahoma and 
Arkansas. Model guidance suggests this wave will close off at 
500mb as it lifts northeastward across southern Missouri and 
into southern Illinois by late this evening and overnight. 
Strong differential cyclonic vorticity advection (dCVA) ahead of
this feature will peak over central and southern Illinois mid- 
to-late this afternoon. This forcing for ascent will align with 
the right-entrance region of a modest 70-kt upper-level jet 
streak, interacting with a weakly unstable environment. The GFS 
is advertising MLCAPE values near 500 J/kg across central 
Illinois by Friday afternoon. However, forecast soundings depict
elongated, 'skinny' CAPE profiles, which should limit updraft 
strength. Combined with negligible deep-layer shear, the overall
severe threat remains very low. In fact, weak updrafts may 
struggle to grow deep enough to support lightning. Despite the 
low severe risk, the proximity of the closed upper low does 
present a conditional threat for funnel clouds. The RAP 
highlights a few pockets of non-supercell tornado parameters 
around 1-3 grazing our southern CWA border, though the primary 
focus for this activity remains closer to the core of the low 
within the LSX forecast area.

     Saturday and Sunday...
By Saturday, the closed upper low is projected to open into a 
trough as it slowly moves eastward along the lower Ohio Valley. 
A few lingering light showers are possible east of I-57, but the
vast majority of central Illinois will remain dry. To the 
northwest, a cold front will advance across the Upper Midwest on
Saturday. An associated thermal ridge, characterized by 850mb 
temperatures of 18-20C, will surge across central Illinois ahead
of the front. This will support a quick rebound in temperatures, 
with widespread highs in the upper 80s and a few locations 
hitting 90. As the front stalls over the region on Sunday, a 
sharp thermal gradient will develop across the local area. Highs
north of the Illinois River are forecast to sit around 80, 
while southern areas south of I-70 soar into the lower 90s. 
While a few light showers or sprinkles cannot be ruled out near 
the front, a prominent 700mb warm nose will keep deep convection
capped.

     Monday through Wednesday...
An active and unsettled weather pattern is anticipated for the 
first half of next week. A high-amplitude upper-level wave is 
progged to lift from the Pacific Northwest across the Canadian 
Rockies Sunday night into Monday. In response, a deep surface 
low will develop and trek from the Canadian Prairies toward 
Hudson Bay between Monday and Tuesday. An associated warm front 
will lift across the Great Plains Sunday night, acting as a 
focus for nocturnal convection. Some decaying activity could 
linger into portions of central Illinois as the warm front lifts
northward through the area on Monday. A better opportunity for 
widespread showers and thunderstorms arrives Tuesday into 
Wednesday as the trailing cold front pushes into and stalls 
across the Midwest. A sharp north-to-south temperature gradient 
will establish itself across the CWA, with highs ranging from 
the upper 70s north to the lower 90s south. This period will 
require close monitoring for potential severe weather, as the 
upper-level jet dips into the Great Lakes, boosting deep-layer 
shear across the stalled boundary.

     Thursday and Friday...
Unsettled weather looks to persist late next week as the 
baroclinic zone is progged to linger across the Midwest, serving
as a focus for daily precipitation chances. Model solutions 
begin to diverge regarding the exact placement of this frontal 
boundary by Thursday and Friday; the GFS lifts the front 
northward into the Great Lakes, whereas the ECMWF and GEM keep 
the boundary stalled directly over the Midwest. While details 
regarding timing and location remain low-confidence, the primary
